name: NMN
lead: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a biosynthetic intermediate in the production of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), a coenzyme involved in redox reactions and a substrate for signalling enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs [1][2]. In the body it is made from nicotinamide by the enzyme NAMPT, or from nicotinamide riboside by nicotinamide riboside kinases, and is converted to NAD+ by NMNAT enzymes [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement and, in some products, as a topical skincare ingredient [3].

NMN is marketed for healthy ageing, energy and skin appearance, based on the observation that NAD+ levels fall with age in several tissues and that restoring them improves function in rodents [2][4][5]. Human trials have generally reported that oral NMN raises blood NAD levels and is tolerated over weeks to months, with more mixed or modest results for functional outcomes; reviews state that evidence for anti-ageing effects in people is limited [6][7][8].

Its regulatory status in the United States has been contested: Wikipedia reports that the FDA determined in 2022 that NMN could not be sold as a supplement because it was under investigation as a drug, and later rescinded that determination for the beta-NMN form [1]. In looksmaxxing and physique communities NMN appears as an add-on in longevity and recovery supplement lists [9][10].

paras: NMN is a nucleotide formed by attaching a phosphoribose group to nicotinamide. It is a rate-limiting intermediate in mammalian NAD+ synthesis through the NAMPT pathway [11][12]. It occurs naturally in foods such as edamame, broccoli, cabbage, cucumber and avocado at roughly 1 mg per 100 g, which Wikipedia describes as too low to supply amounts used in studies [1].

Wikipedia reports that a transporter called Slc12a8 was proposed to carry NMN into mouse intestinal cells, but this has been challenged and remains unsettled; reviews also discuss whether NMN is first converted to nicotinamide riboside outside cells before uptake [1][13]. NMN can be broken down extracellularly by the enzyme CD38, whose rising activity with age has itself been proposed as a driver of age-related NAD decline [1][14].

NMN is promoted for skin appearance and rejuvenation, both as an oral supplement and as an ingredient in topical products; a US label for a face cream combining NMN with ectoine directs users to apply it to the face as a final skincare step and warns against use on wounds or inflamed skin [3]. No published randomised trial in the source of human studies reviewed assesses facial appearance or skin ageing as a primary outcome of NMN.
Physique-oriented forum users mention NMN alongside creatine, L-carnitine and turmeric as part of leaner-looking or endurance-oriented regimens, though such reports are anecdotal [9][15].

NMN has no approved drug indication. It has been studied in healthy middle-aged and older adults, prediabetes, exercise performance, sleep, vascular stiffness and, in registered trials, immune ageing, ovarian reserve and polycystic ovary syndrome [8][11][16][17][18][19][20].

Supplemental NMN is proposed to raise NAD+ levels, which in turn supports sirtuin and mitochondrial function [2][13]. In mouse studies, NMN improved glucose handling in diet- and age-induced diabetes and long-term administration mitigated age-associated physiological decline [21][5]. Reviews caution that NAD+ metabolism is complex, that animal findings do not always transfer to humans, and that factors affecting the success or risks of NAD+ supplementation remain poorly understood [22][4].

A 2023 review of human clinical trials of NMN concluded that it appears safe over the periods studied and raises NAD+ status, while noting that most evidence for anti-ageing effects comes from cell and animal work and that human trials are few and short [6]. A 2022 review similarly discussed promise and safety concerns [7].

A multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 80 healthy middle-aged adults tested several oral doses for 60 days, reporting effects on NAD levels, walking and other measures of health [8]. A 10-week randomised trial in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese found that NMN increased insulin-stimulated muscle insulin signalling and sensitivity, as reported in Science [11]. A trial in older adults reported higher blood NAD levels, maintained walking speed and improved sleep quality [23], while a 12-week trial in older Japanese adults assessed sleep, fatigue and physical performance [24]. A randomised study in amateur runners reported enhanced aerobic capacity [17], and a randomised trial examined arterial stiffness after long-term NMN [16]. Some of these trials were funded or supported by supplement manufacturers.

Registered trials include studies in diminished ovarian reserve, repeated IVF failure, polycystic ovary syndrome, immunosenescence in metabolic disease, frailty and exercise tolerance in older adults, and a safety study in a rare congenital disorder of glycosylation [19][25][20][18][26][27].

Short-term human trials have reported good tolerability, and a Keio University single-dose study found doses of up to 500 mg safe in men, according to Wikipedia [6][1]. Mild gastrointestinal effects and flushing have been reported with NAD+ precursors in general [28]. Long-term safety in humans is not established, and reviews raise theoretical questions about boosting NAD+ in people with existing cancers or other conditions, which remain unresolved [22][7]. Product quality and composition vary between suppliers [7].

According to Wikipedia, in 2022 the FDA took the position that NMN could not be marketed as a dietary supplement because it was being investigated as a pharmaceutical drug, and this determination was later rescinded for the beta form [1]. Dietary supplement companies have promoted NMN heavily for anti-ageing, a marketing pattern described by Wikipedia as outpacing human proof of benefit [1].

subs.h: Use in physique and longevity communities
paras: On T Nation, users report adding NMN to creatine and electrolyte drinks, listing it among daily supplements next to ubiquinol and taurine, and asking whether it can rejuvenate arteries for ageing lifters or heal intestinal damage [15][10][29][30]. A user on testosterone therapy who had begun both resveratrol and NMN reported a spike in estradiol and wondered about a connection; no study cited here examines that [31].

lore.intro: NMN is discussed in training forums as a longevity and recovery add-on, usually alongside creatine, CoQ10 or resveratrol [15][10][31].

claims.claim: NMN restores NAD+ and slows or reverses ageing
claims.believers: Proponents argue that NAD+ declines with age and that topping it up rejuvenates tissues, and forum users describe taking it for joints, circulation and looking leaner [9][29].
claims.experts: Rodent studies show benefits, while human trials show raised NAD levels with modest or mixed functional results, and reviews state that anti-ageing effects in people are not established [5][6][7].

claims.believers: A T Nation user cited a video claiming NMN rejuvenates arteries and veins and asked other older lifters whether they take it [29].
claims.experts: A randomised trial examined arterial stiffness after long-term supplementation, and mouse work links NAD+ and vascular ageing, but no definitive human result is established [16][33].

claims.claim: NMN could heal intestinal damage in inflammatory bowel disease
claims.believers: A forum user asked whether it could heal intestinal damage in a thread about steroid cycles with IBD [30].
claims.experts: No published human trial cited here has tested NMN for inflammatory bowel disease.

claims.believers: Some users report running feeling better and adding NMN to training drinks [9][15].
claims.experts: One randomised study in amateur runners reported improved aerobic capacity and another in older adults reported maintained walking speed, but trials are small and short [17][23].
